title: Australia Regulates Supplements Like Drugs, but Nobody Checks If They Work
dek: Australia puts supplements and medicines under the same regulator, which looks strict; but efficacy is neither reviewed before market nor tested during production — the impression of "good" was implanted by marketing and cross-border policy.
why: The first half's regulatory breakdown is solid, and the second half's chain from marketing to daigou policy is complete; but the middle section has a lot of transcription garbage, and the information density is uneven.
who: Investors and founders looking at consumer brands, supplements and cross-border e-commerce, as well as people doing brand marketing and concerned about regulatory arbitrage.

points.h: Australians taking pills is a tradition
points.body: The soil for Australia's supplement industry isn't the natural environment, it's four social habits: a vast, sparsely populated land leading to self-medication, pharmacists also doing diagnosis and dispensing, naturopathic industry organizations existing as early as the 1920s, and health food stores similar to food-as-medicine shops. Stacked together, these four made Australians accustomed to "solving health problems without going to the hospital." Black Moth (澳佳宝) started as a naturopathic clinic, and only after the second generation took over did it translate that into products the mainstream system could recognize — for example, turning "take a spoonful of fish oil a day" into standardized fish oil capsules.

points.h: The contract manufacturer is the industry's foundation
points.body: Pen Pharmaceuticals, which appeared in 1974, was Australia's first company focused on contract manufacturing for supplements, and by around 2003 it was responsible for about 70% of Australia's vitamin, mineral and herbal product production. Its value lay in process know-how: tablets, compound ingredients, the rubber-and-oil seal of soft capsules, the mixing uniformity of powders, the stability of liquids — each is its own set of solutions. In the 1980s-90s a new generation of contract manufacturers extended services in both directions, moving from pure production (CMO) to CDMO covering formulation, ingredients, trial production, labeling, packaging, testing, and registration for export. The brand only needs to give a concept, and the factory can turn it into a marketable product.

points.h: Registration means nobody looks before market
points.body: Australia legislated in 1989, putting medicines and supplements under the TGA, and all products must obtain an AUST number. Most supplements enter the AUSTL category: they can only use low-risk ingredients permitted by the TGA, can only make low-level health efficacy claims, and companies can get a number just by applying themselves — the TGA does no pre-market review, only post-market spot checks. By around 2010 Australia had about ten thousand complementary medicines, of which nearly 98% belonged to this registration system. Only prescription drugs, over-the-counter drugs and a small number of high-risk supplements enter the AUSTR tier, which requires the TGA to assess safety, quality and efficacy in advance.

points.h: It looks strict, but is actually loose
points.body: Putting the contract manufacturing and regulatory lines together: GMP only ensures the contract manufacturer produces stably according to the standards the brand gives, and that problems can be traced to batch recalls — it itself is not responsible for product efficacy. The TGA side only handles declarations and issuing batch numbers, and efficacy is explained by the brand itself. So the saying "Australia regulates supplements like drugs" is itself not wrong, but it is misleading: the regulatory method is the same, but the regulatory standard for the efficacy part differs enormously. The entire system does no effective upfront supervision of the product's actual effect, and there is a risk of disconnect between the brand and product efficacy.

points.h: The marketing learned from Centrum, not invented
points.body: CEO Radek Sali, who took office in 2008, did not come up with a marketing plan out of thin air. In his industry research he found that the best-selling peer was Centrum, and feedback from retailers was: Centrum didn't give terminals high profits, but it was unstoppable because it ran ads frantically on TV all year, had good athlete endorsements, and consumers would ask for it by name when entering pharmacies. Sali wanted to replicate this at Swisse. He first invested in Australia's national sport, cricket — the men's cricket team captain, buying only very short ad slots during the hottest summer cricket broadcasts, so that even with a limited budget he could appear at important moments. But the female-dominated sales channel was not impressed; some buyers didn't watch cricket themselves and didn't know that athlete. He asked his mother what shows she liked, and she said she liked a dance variety show, and the strategy shifted to entertainment content mentions.

Swisse's bigger round of publicity leveraged Oprah and Ellen, and signed a three-year deal with actress Nicole Kidman, pushing its reach from Australia to the US. By 2012, Swisse had 25 brand ambassadors, had shot more than 80 TV commercials in the previous 12 months, annual revenue reached 183 million Australian dollars, and marketing spend was 40-50 million Australian dollars a year — said to have been at one point the highest marketing spend among Australian consumer brands. Its ads did not emphasize efficacy and ingredients, but mainly presented a state of being energetic, positively self-disciplined, and good-looking — turning health into a lifestyle consumers aspire to. In 2012 Swisse gained more than 20% market share in Australian supermarket channels and more than 10% in pharmacy channels.

points.h: The growth point was found in Chinese pharmacies
points.body: Swisse spent a lot of money on the US market without much success, and after returning to Australia found that Swisse sold very well in pharmacies in Chinese-concentrated areas — some stores sold ten times as much as ordinary stores — because international students and Chinese immigrants bought in bulk to take back to China or resell online, that is, daigou. In 2015 two policy shifts appeared: in March the Hangzhou Cross-Border E-Commerce Comprehensive Pilot Zone was approved, and in June China and Australia signed a free trade agreement, which officially took effect in December that year. The FTA mainly affected general trade; Australian official statistics put the tariff on vitamins and supplements generally at 3% to 10%, while Black Moth itself estimated an average rate of 20%, and after the agreement it was said at the time that it could drop to zero within four years. Cross-border e-commerce goes through bonded warehouses, platforms buy in bulk, logistics time and cost drop sharply, and such goods are treated as personal use in policy, so they don't need to go through the supplement import registration and filing process.

points.h: The brand was bought, the impression stayed
points.body: In September 2015, Hong Kong-listed Biostime completed the acquisition of a controlling stake in Swisse, and two years later completed a full acquisition, with a deal size of about 1.7 billion Australian dollars, or 8.7 billion RMB. For Swisse the deal had little premium; for Biostime it added a large chunk of business revenue and imagination. Now all those Swisse ads in Hunan TV variety shows are theoretically paid for by a Chinese supplement company, but the brand can still say it is an Australian supplement brand, and consumers can still apply their past vague good impression of Australia to it — the core value of the acquisition, to a large extent, settles in the brand goodwill part.

quotes.text: The GMP system itself is not responsible for the product's efficacy; it can only prove that the contract manufacturer produced according to the standards given by the brand.
The whole system actually looks strict but is loose in practice, especially for the efficacy part.
This looseness means that no part of the system has conducted any effective upfront supervision of the product's actual effect.
It doesn't emphasize efficacy and ingredients; it mainly presents a state of being energetic, positively self-disciplined, and good-looking — turning health into a lifestyle consumers aspire to.
The supplement industry doesn't have any particular barrier to entry; if everyone doesn't compete on marketing, for now they haven't found the next thing to compete on.
When consumers face something they are unfamiliar with, they easily string together other familiar and credible concepts to understand this unfamiliar thing.

We easily remember some particularly simple concepts or judgments, so simple that you forget there were originally so many layers of logic behind them. So the more a business idea resembles common sense, the more it's worth asking: how did it come about, and how did it become so-called common sense?
